meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If all the girls who attended the Yale prom were laid end to end, I wouldn't be at all surprised'?
meta.ogDescription: The only contemporary record is page 149 of Woollcott's While Rome Burns (1934) — and it says "Mrs. Parker said, she wouldn't be at all surprised," not "I."

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet and critic; founding Algonquin Round Table wit
answer.sourceLine: The only contemporary record is second-hand: Alexander Woollcott printed the quip on page 149 of While Rome Burns (The Viking Press, March 1934) as reported speech — “If all the girls attending it were laid end to end, Mrs. Parker said, she wouldn’t be at all surprised.” Quote Investigator calls that 1934 credit substantive and finds no close match before it ↗. But Parker never wrote the line herself, and the familiar first-person wording — “who attended the Yale prom … I wouldn’t be at all surprised” — is a later smoothing of Woollcott’s sentence, not a transcript.
answer.confidenceText: Documented as hers in 1934 — but by a friend, in reported speech, and not in this wording.

source.excerpt: And there was that wholesale libel on a Yale prom. If all the girls attending it were laid end to end, Mrs. Parker said, she wouldn’t be at all surprised.
trail: 1843 — the frame exists. Quote Investigator points to a Liverpool Mercury item ↗ measuring printed columns laid end to end from Liverpool to London. The measurement gag is Victorian newspaper filler, decades before anyone thought to make it filthy.

1927–1931 — it goes collegiate, then risqué. Judge magazine ran “If all the college boys who slept in class were placed end to end they would be much more comfortable” in August 1927, and by 1931 a book advertisement was joking that if a character’s lovers were laid end to end it would put them in a very awkward position — both catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗.

March 1934 — the anchor. Alexander Woollcott’s While Rome Burns reaches print, and on page 149, inside his portrait “Our Mrs. Parker,” the Yale prom line is credited to her. The scanned book is readable at the Internet Archive ↗; its copyright page records “PUBLISHED MARCH 1934” and sixteen printings by October 1935. This is the earliest close match anyone has found.

1945–2003 — the drift. Samuel Hopkins Adams gives it as “I wouldn’t be a bit surprised” in 1945; Corey Ford moves it to Princeton in 1967; Scott Meredith relocates it to Smith and Bennington in 1974; Dominique Enright restores something close to Woollcott in 2003. The sequence is laid out citation by citation at Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: Read it closely: Woollcott is narrating, not transcribing. The remark arrives inside his own sentence, with “Mrs. Parker said” wedged into the middle and the verdict in the third person — she wouldn’t be at all surprised. The familiar version rewrites that as a clean first-person line. The paragraph is a run of Parker asides; the sentence just before this one is her suspicion that a friend hurt herself “sliding down a barrister.”

While Rome Burns was published in March 1934 by The Viking Press, and its copyright page reads “COPYRIGHT 1934 BY ALEXANDER WOOLLCOTT” — comfortably inside the era where US works remain protected, so the text is treated here as in copyright and quoted only in the brief extract needed to document the attribution. Parker’s spoken remark has no separate published source of her own; her literary estate passed to Martin Luther King Jr. and, after his death, to the NAACP.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.kicker: The wit at the head of the table
author.heading: Who was Dorothy Parker?
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893) wrote theatre criticism for Vanity Fair until her dismissal in January 1920, then joined the board of editors at The New Yorker when Harold Ross founded it in 1925, contributing drama reviews, verse and short fiction. She was a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, the lunch circle of New York writers whose reputation for savage one-liners rests heavily on what its members later remembered and wrote down. That is precisely the problem with her most famous quips: Parker’s published work is fully documented, but her talk survives mainly through friends’ memoirs. She died on 7 June 1967 and left her estate to Martin Luther King Jr., and on his death to the NAACP.

misattribution.heading: What gets changed in the retelling
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong name on a real quote. Parker is very probably the source. The trouble is that almost nobody quotes her the way the only contemporary record actually reads — and the joke’s skeleton was doing the rounds long before she got to it.

items.who: “… who attended the Yale prom … I wouldn’t be at all surprised”
items.why: Woollcott wrote it as reported speech folded into his own narration: “If all the girls attending it were laid end to end, Mrs. Parker said, she wouldn’t be at all surprised.” The circulating version converts “attending it” into “who attended the Yale prom” and “she” into “I,” producing a clean first-person epigram that appears in no 1934 text. Wikiquote still prints Woollcott’s original phrasing ↗.

Samuel Hopkins Adams gave it as “If all the girls who attended the Yale Prom this year were laid end to end, I wouldn’t be a bit surprised” in his 1945 biography of Woollcott, per Quote Investigator ↗. “A bit” and “at all” have been swapping places ever since, and neither is more authentic than the other — only Woollcott’s is first.

The school will not stay put. Quote Investigator records Corey Ford setting it at Princeton in 1967, Robert Drennan turning it into ‘all those sweet young things present’ in 1968, and Scott Meredith relocating it to Smith and Bennington in 1974 ↗. A specific that drifts this freely is a specific nobody is checking.

The “laid end to end” comparison was a stock newspaper device long before the Round Table. Quote Investigator cites an 1843 Liverpool Mercury item measuring printed columns laid end to end from Liverpool to London ↗, collegiate gags in Judge magazine in 1927, and a 1931 book advertisement joking that if a character’s lovers were laid end to end it would put them in a very awkward position. Parker’s contribution is the swerve, not the frame.

In July 1945 The New Yorker credited the operetta Marinka with “If all your lovers were laid end to end, I’d be very much pleased,” as recorded by Quote Investigator ↗. It is a cousin of the gag rather than a challenger to Parker’s version, but it shows how many hands were working the same joke.

misattribution.truthLine: The whole case for Parker is one second-hand sentence on page 149 of a 1934 book written by a friend — substantive evidence, in Quote Investigator’s judgement ↗, with nothing closer found before it. Credit her; just don’t pass off the popular wording as a transcript.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The joke is a trapdoor. On the surface it is an innocent measurement gag — the kind of thing that had been filling newspaper columns since the 1840s, where you line up an enormous quantity of something and report how far it stretches. Parker’s version refuses to complete the sentence. She sets up the measurement, then declines to measure anything, and the whole payload lands in the second meaning of “laid.” It is a punchline that makes the listener do the indecent part.

That structure is also why the line travels so badly. Because the joke lives in the rhythm rather than in any particular fact, the specifics are free to drift — and they have. In retellings collected by Quote Investigator ↗ the setting moves from a Yale prom to Princeton to “Smith and Bennington” to a vague “all those present,” and the tag flips between “I wouldn’t be at all surprised,” “I wouldn’t be a bit surprised” and “I wouldn’t be surprised.” The core survives every retelling; nothing else does.
context.detailsSummary: Why Woollcott’s essay carries so much of Parker’s reputation
detailsBody: “Our Mrs. Parker” is a portrait written by a friend and fellow Round Table member for a bestselling collection, and it is where a striking number of Parker’s best-known spoken lines first reach print. On the same page 149 Woollcott sets down her line about the guest who “speaks eighteen languages, and can’t say No in any of them,” the suspicion that a friend hurt herself “sliding down a barrister,” and the Yale prom remark — three of her most-quoted quips, in a single paragraph, all inside Woollcott’s narration rather than in quotation marks she can be held to.

That is not a reason to reject the attribution. Woollcott was there, he published while Parker was very much alive and capable of objecting, and no earlier claimant has surfaced. It is a reason to be precise about what kind of evidence it is: a warm, second-hand, undated memoir sentence — and to notice that the version everybody repeats is not the sentence he actually wrote.
context.pull: She sets up the measurement, then declines to measure anything.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes that Alexander Woollcott credited Dorothy Parker with this quip in 1934, that the evidence was substantive, and that QI found no close matches before 1934; it also documents the 1843 Liverpool Mercury 'laid end to end' item, 1927 Judge magazine variants, a 1931 book advertisement, Samuel Hopkins Adams's 1945 'I wouldn't be a bit surprised' version, a July 1945 New Yorker credit to the operetta Marinka, Corey Ford's 1967 Princeton setting, Robert Drennan's 1968 'sweet young things present', Scott Meredith's 1974 'Smith and Bennington', and Dominique Enright's 2003 version.

The scanned copy of Alexander Woollcott's While Rome Burns (The Viking Press, New York) contains on page 149, within the essay 'Our Mrs. Parker', the text: 'And there was that wholesale libel on a Yale prom. If all the girls attending it were laid end to end, Mrs. Parker said, she wouldn't be at all surprised.' The copyright page reads 'PUBLISHED MARCH 1934' with sixteen printings listed through October 1935, and 'COPYRIGHT 1934 BY ALEXANDER WOOLLCOTT'.

Wikiquote lists the line under its Quotes section, in the subsection headed 'Our Mrs Parker' (1934), in Woollcott's reported-speech wording, sourced to his biographical essay in While Rome Burns (1934); the page separately warns that a great many misquotations are attributed to Dorothy Parker.

Dorothy Parker lived 22 August 1893 to 7 June 1967, was an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction, was a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, was a Vanity Fair theatre critic dismissed on 11 January 1920, was part of The New Yorker's board of editors when Harold Ross founded it in 1925, and bequeathed her estate to Martin Luther King Jr. and upon his death to the NAACP.
While Rome Burns is a 1934 book collecting Alexander Woollcott's writings for The New Yorker and other magazines, which became a bestseller after he promoted it on his radio show.
Open Library's record for While Rome Burns lists first publication by The Viking Press in 1934, with later editions including Viking 1935, Grosset & Dunlap 1936, Penguin 1937 and Pocket Books 1942.

Alexander Woollcott was born 19 January 1887 and died 23 January 1943, was a drama critic for The New York Times, was a critic and commentator for The New Yorker, was a radio personality, and was a member of the Algonquin Round Table.
